DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Food Waste Collection

**Overall:** The pilot design is good, and the cost arithmetic in Table 2 is correct. However, the study misreads its own pilot data and uses a participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot results. It also overlooks a treatment capacity limit that it states itself. Once these are corrected, the service is probably **not** fully covered by the provisional funding, and flats clearly need a different approach. The recommendation needs revising before it goes to Cabinet.

## Major issues

### 1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types

Table 1 shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**. Houses participated at more than three times the rate of flats. The study's conclusion in section 2, which your summary repeats, is the opposite of what its own data shows.

This is a common pattern: flats usually lack outdoor space for caddies and need communal food waste bins, different collection points and targeted communication. The pilot is actually good evidence that **flats need a separate approach**, which is the opposite of what the study recommends.

### 2. The district projection uses a participation rate that isn't in the pilot

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate," but Table 1 gives **57%** overall. The figure of 64% doesn't appear anywhere.

Thornbury has the same housing mix as the pilot (20% flats), so the pilot's rates by housing type can be applied directly:

| | Households | Participation | Participating | kg per week | Tonnes per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 27,456 | 1.9 | 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 2,184 | 1.4 | 159 |
| **Total** | **52,000** | **57%** | **29,640** | | **~2,870** |

That's about **2,870 tonnes, not 3,290**, an overstatement of about 13%. The pilot also ran for only six months, and participation in new services often dips once the novelty wears off, so even 2,870 tonnes may be optimistic.

### 3. Brookfield can only take 1,800 tonnes

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected projection exceeds this by about 1,070 tonnes, and the study's own figure exceeds it by about 1,490 tonnes. Yet the £243,000 saving assumes *every* tonne goes to Brookfield at £38.

The surplus would have to go to the plant 46 miles away, with longer journeys, more vehicle and crew time, and an unknown gate fee. The study prices none of this. Incinerating separately collected food waste is not a realistic fallback either. So "treatment is local," as your summary puts it, is only true for about 60% of the projected tonnage.

### 4. The service is probably not fully funded

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Compared with £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As in the study (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 within it |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t), all at £74 saving (not actually possible) | £212,500 | £520,900 | **£900 over** |
| Corrected tonnage, saving only on Brookfield's 1,800 t | £133,200 | £600,200 | **£80,200 over**, plus haulage for the surplus |

Even the best case with corrected tonnage slightly exceeds the allocation, and the realistic case is clearly over budget. In addition, the funding is described as "provisional" and "indicated," and the study doesn't say whether it is guaranteed beyond the first year.

### 5. "Every cost line is shown" overstates the cost table

The arithmetic in Table 2 is correct: £990,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400, 12 × £34,000 = £408,000, and the total is £733,400. But likely costs are missing:

- **Staff on-costs:** It isn't stated whether £34,000 includes employer pension and National Insurance. If it doesn't, the crew costs are understated by roughly 25–30%.
- **Relief cover** for holidays and sickness. Six crews with no relief can't run a weekly service all year.
- **A spare vehicle**, or hire cover for breakdowns.
- **Supervision and management.**
- **Vehicle financing costs:** Depreciation alone ignores borrowing costs.
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in section 6.
- **Replacement caddies** and **ongoing liners** after the first three months, if they aren't already in the £88,000.
- **Transport to the second plant** for tonnage over 1,800.

## Other issues

- **Statutory deadline:** In England, the weekly food waste requirement under Simpler Recycling applied from 31 March 2026, apart from councils with agreed transitional arrangements. If Thornbury has such an arrangement, the study should say so. If it doesn't, the study should explain the April 2027 start.
- **No slack in the timetable:** Vehicles arrive in March and collections start on 5 April. In the same month, crews are being trained and caddies delivered to 52,000 households. A late vehicle delivery would delay the launch, and the study needs a contingency plan.
- **Satisfaction figure:** The 81% comes from "surveyed pilot households." Give the response rate, and note that participating households are more likely to respond.
- **Food waste per household:** The "All" row's 1.9 kg is really about 1.86 kg when weighted. That's fine as rounding, but it shows the flats' lower yield. The district projection rightly applies 1.4 kg for flats in the corrected version.
- **Seasonality:** January to June may not reflect yields across the full year. The study should say whether summer or Christmas yields are expected to differ.
- **Strengths:** The pilot design (mixed wards, weekly measurement by housing type), contamination below 2%, falling missed collections, and working the timetable back from the vehicle lead time are all good.

## Your summary versus the document

- **"Participation held up across houses and flats":** It didn't: 66% compared with 21%.
- **"Treatment is local":** Only up to 1,800 tonnes.
- **"Every cost line is shown":** Several are missing.
- **"Fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation":** Only with the incorrect 64% figure and by ignoring the capacity limit.
- **"The financial analysis is complete and transparent":** It's transparent, which is helpful, but not complete.

## Suggested changes

1. Rewrite the participation conclusion and propose a separate service design for flats, such as communal bins and targeted engagement.
2. Recalculate tonnage using the pilot rates by housing type, and test lower participation as a sensitivity.
3. Cost the tonnage above Brookfield's capacity, including haulage and the second plant's gate fee, until 2029.
4. Complete the cost table with on-costs, relief cover, a spare vehicle, supervision, financing and the helpline.
5. Restate the net cost as a range, and confirm the status and duration of the funding.
6. Clarify the statutory position, and add contingency to the timetable.

The case for the service is still strong, because the pilot shows it works for houses. But Cabinet should approve it knowing the true cost and the separate approach needed for flats.
